sourceRanges.firstLine: Four businessmen from Ireland bought Ireland.
sourceRanges.lastLine: More than twenty years after the first island rose out of the water, there's still no power cable running out to them.

ending.text: So who was telling the truth about the world? Full story's on the channel.

sourceRanges.firstLine: You see, the islands weren't really sold as land.
sourceRanges.lastLine: "So, what do you do?" "Oh, I own Ireland." And technically, that wasn't even a lie.

sourceRanges.firstLine: In two thousand and nine, right in the middle of all this, a British property developer named Safi Qurashi bought the island called Great Britain.

sourceRanges.firstLine: And to secure the deal, he handed over cheques.
sourceRanges.lastLine: Three cheques, worth around one hundred and eighty-nine million dirhams, bounced.

sourceRanges.firstLine: In January two thousand and ten, he was sentenced to seven years in jail.

sourceRanges.firstLine: He was released in two thousand and twelve, and later, Dubai's highest court quashed the rest of his sentence.
sourceRanges.lastLine: But by then, the man who bought Great Britain had spent his time on the map behind bars.

ending.text: And he wasn't the only one taking Nakheel to court. Full story's on the channel.

sourceRanges.firstLine: First rule of island life here: bring your own electricity.
sourceRanges.lastLine: Anyone building on an island had to make their own power with diesel generators.

sourceRanges.firstLine: There's no sewer to plug into and no power line to connect.
sourceRanges.lastLine: Before you build a single villa, you have to build a tiny town's worth of pipes and cables, on your own, in the sea.

ending.text: And one man decided to try anyway. Full story's on the channel.
